AMERICANISM: From Nativist Panic to Imperial Heresy

How Protestant Patriotism Became a Geopolitical Weapon Against Catholic Civilization

Americanism did not begin as a harmless form of patriotic self-congratulation. Long before it was condemned as a theological error by Leo XIII, it had already taken shape as a nativist moral panic. In the antebellum decades—just as Irish and German Catholic immigration surged—“Americanism” acquired a restrictive, quasi-ideological meaning: the belief that true American identity was inseparable from Anglo-Protestant culture.

This early Americanism was explicitly anti-Catholic. It treated Catholic immigrants as a foreign, corrupt, authoritarian element incapable of assimilation into the “true American spirit.” Nativist mobs burned churches and the suspicion grew that Catholicism—hierarchical, traditional, universal—was inherently incompatible with the liberal, individualist ethos of the Republic.

That tension did not vanish. It metastasized.

By the late 19th century, the same spirit of Protestant nativism had evolved into something larger and more ambitious: a political-theological project to refashion Catholicism itself into a civic religion compatible with American liberalism. And this is precisely what Pope Leo XIII condemned in Testem Benevolentiae (1899).

The “heresy of Americanism” was not merely a doctrinal footnote. It was a geopolitical doctrine, emerging at the very moment when the United States was preparing to eclipse the last remnants of the Spanish Catholic Empire. As Washington stoked the Black Legend—depicting Spain as cruel, backward, despotic, and unfit for empire—it seized Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines under the pretext of liberating them from medieval Catholic darkness.

Americanism was the theological arm of this project.
It demanded that Catholics in the United States:
•Subordinate the Church’s universality to the Republic’s exceptionalism
•Treat democratic sentiment as a corrective to doctrine
•Replace Catholic historical memory with a Protestantized “Western civilization” mythology
•Accept the United States as the spiritual standard-bearer of the Hemisphere

It made the Cross an accessory for the flag. It made Rome optional and Washington essential.

Leo XIII condemned it as he recognized that Americanism sought to transform the Church into a servant of a rising liberal empire—an empire built in direct opposition to the Spanish Catholic world it had just conquered.

And now, more than a century later, that heresy has returned with renewed force.

When the U.S. Department of Labor declares that “the fight for Western Civilization has begun and Americanism will prevail,” it is not an innocent flourish of patriotic enthusiasm. It is the resurrection of the old formula:
equating “the West” exclusively with the Anglo-Protestant tradition, and banishing the Catholic, Hispanic, and Mediterranean foundations of the Hemisphere from civilizational legitimacy.

This is no accident. It appears precisely as Washington accelerates a supercharged Monroe Doctrine, preparing the ideological terrain for a possible intervention in Venezuela. The narrative is familiar: disciplined, rational, liberty-bearing Americanism must prevail over the supposedly corrupt, chaotic, backward, and ungovernable heirs of the Spanish world.

The Black Legend is not believed.
It is used. Empires do not operate on truth; they operate on myths that justify domination.

Which raises the unavoidable question:

Will Pope Leo XIV follow the example of his great namesake?

Will he expose its nature as an attempt to subordinate Catholic civilization to the imperial ideology of the United States?

Will he denounce its fusion of Protestantized morality, manifest destiny, and civilizational chauvinism?

Or will Rome remain silent while Americanism again frames itself as the guardian of “Western civilization,” even as it prepares to extinguish yet another Catholic nation’s sovereignty?

BAYAN: POLICE BLOCKED PREPARATIONS FOR LUNETA RALLY

READ: Progressive coalition Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) says the police blocked the preparations for the anti-corruption protest to be conducted at the Luneta Park in Manila on Sunday, Nov. 30.

BAYAN, among the organizers of the rally, says they were not given with a permit, the same situation during their Sept. 21 rally, but the protest was coordinated with the Manila government and the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority. It cites the announcement of road closures and the setting up of MMDA portalets in the area as signs of the coordination with authorities.

Still, BAYAN and their allied groups say they will continue to gather at the Luneta for their Nov. 30 rally.

📸 BAYAN/Facebook

The Cross-Border Remittance Flip: Stablecoins Cracked the 6 Percent Wall

Global remittances have always carried a quiet cost that everyone recognized but few questioned. Families depended on money sent from abroad, yet every transfer included a toll that felt impossible to avoid. The world ran on a 6 percent average fee because the system offered no real alternative.

Stablecoins changed the assumptions behind the entire market.

Their spread across remittance-heavy regions has created a new baseline for global money movement. The cost structure looks different. The speed looks different. The behavior of both users and enterprises reflects this shift. The story is no longer about experimentation. It is about a parallel set of rails emerging with better economics and broader reach.

The result is a clean break from a model that dominated for decades.

Fee Structure: The First Major Fracture

The World Bank’s 2025 data pinned bank and MTO remittance costs at 6.49 percent on average. Those fees persisted across nearly every major corridor.

Stablecoins introduced a different profile:

- Typical all-in costs between 0.5 and 3 percent
- Certain corridors landing comfortably below 1 percent
- Savings that reach 30 to 60 percent on high-volume routes

The math rewrites itself quickly at consumer scale. Regular monthly transfers become cheaper. Diaspora communities retain more of what they earn. Cross-border gig workers can move income with fewer losses. The economic impact is immediate and measurable.

This is where the flip truly begins.

Adoption Momentum: A Pattern That Widens Each Quarter

Usage trends show consistent acceleration. The past year produced several striking data points:

- In the U.S., 26 percent of remittance users turned to stablecoins
- Across Latin America, 71 percent of stablecoin holders rely on them for cross-border payments
- Inflation-heavy markets treat stablecoins as dependable digital dollars rather than speculative instruments

What stands out is the composition of users. These are not traders chasing volatility. They are workers, families, small business owners, and freelancers choosing a tool that aligns with their daily needs. The motivation is utility, not hype.

As the user base expands, the channel becomes the default rather than the alternative.

Enterprise Movement: Remittance Leaders Build on the Rails

The enterprise pivot is now a defining part of the transition.

- Remitly added USDC to improve settlement times and streamline payouts across more than 170 countries
- Aspora scaled from $400 million to $2 billion in volume within one year
- Users on diaspora-focused platforms collectively saved millions due to cheaper settlement costs

These companies are not layering crypto on top of old infrastructure. They are redesigning their internal systems to function on chain. Faster treasury movement means thinner margins can finally work. Transparent fee structures become viable. High-traffic corridors gain new levels of efficiency.

What started among retail users now runs through the decisions of global operators.

Speed: A New Standard for Urgent Payments

International transfers that once lingered for days now move with the tempo of modern communication. Traditional corridors rely on business hours, intermediary approvals, and slow reconciliation cycles. Stablecoins remove all of those constraints.

A worker in Nairobi can receive USDC from a client in another continent and convert it locally within minutes. A freelancer in Southeast Asia gains immediate access to cleared funds instead of waiting through weekend bottlenecks. Informal trade and online work benefit from predictable availability.

When settlement aligns with real-life urgency, behavior follows.

Emerging Markets: Early Leaders Instead of Late Adopters

The strongest adoption is concentrated in regions where financial infrastructure historically lagged behind digital adoption. Chainalysis’ rankings for 2025 place India, Nigeria, the Philippines, and several Latin American markets among the highest users of digital assets.

The reasons are structural:
- Limited banking penetration
- Heavy reliance on mobile devices
- Persistent currency instability
- High remittance dependence

Stablecoins fit these conditions with unusual precision. Merchants use them for payments. Families store value with less fear of depreciation. Workers sidestep outdated systems that previously controlled the pace and cost of their income flow.

The center of gravity for this transition clearly sits in the global south.

Infrastructure Maturity: Rails That Can Handle Scale

Developments in 2025 show a maturing ecosystem rather than an experimental stage.

Visa’s pilot connected merchants and creators to USDC payouts that settle directly to digital wallets. Platforms like Nium extended tokenized liquidity across global corridors. Regulatory clarity strengthened in Brazil, Singapore, and through new frameworks in the U.S.

Stablecoins now operate within standardized compliance environments and integrate with established financial institutions. This foundation enables broader adoption without sacrificing reliability.

The groundwork for true global-scale settlement is now in place.

Final Perspective: The Fee Era That Controlled Remittances Is Losing Its Power

The remittance market functioned with the same economics for years because alternatives were limited. Stablecoins opened a different path. They cut the cost of sending money across borders. They accelerated settlement timelines. They brought inclusion to regions that needed accessible tools more than abstract innovation.

Households keep more of what they earn. Small businesses gain better cash flow. Emerging markets strengthen their financial resilience. The shift started quietly and spread through practical use rather than speculation.

The remittance landscape looks different now. The old structure no longer defines the limits.

A new one is taking hold, and it is expanding faster than anyone projected.

data.raw_text: Little People from the Philippines Island of Lilliput have joined today's protest. Most people don't know there really is a Lilliput island filled with Little People- and it's among the more than 7300 islands in the Philippines archipelago. Their ancestry goes back over 400 years in recorded history. During World War 2, the Little People of the Philippines formed their own guerrilla warfare unit to fight the Japanese, but they didn't get many high profile missions as they were too short, so they got the low profile missions instead. They are not afraid to fight. The US Army made a special vehicle for them, called the half-track, and they carried out dozens of low-profile missions throughout the war, contributing greatly the defeating their invasion of the islands. Lots of cool history out there about them, but the biggest takeaway is that they hate being called Lilliputians. They prefer Lilliputuana and Lilliputuano. The more you know, the more you grow (most people, I mean).
